claim: Newly-formed synaptic vesicles (SVs) are rapidly acidified by vacuolar adenosine triphosphatases (vATPases).
source: Newly-formed synaptic vesicles (SVs) are rapidly acidified by vacuolar adenosine triphosphatases (vATPases), generating a proton electrochemical gradient that drives neurotransmitter loading.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about synaptic vesicle function.

claim: vATPases generate a proton electrochemical gradient that drives neurotransmitter loading.
source: Newly-formed synaptic vesicles (SVs) are rapidly acidified by vacuolar adenosine triphosphatases (vATPases), generating a proton electrochemical gradient that drives neurotransmitter loading.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of vATPases in neurotransmitter loading.

claim: Clathrin-mediated endocytosis is needed for the formation of new SVs.
source: Clathrin-mediated endocytosis is needed for the formation of new SVs, yet it is unclear when endocytosed vesicles acidify and refill at the synapse.
evidence: This is established knowledge about synaptic vesicle formation.

claim: The ATP-induced acidification of CCVs was strikingly reduced in comparison to SVs.
source: We observed that the ATP-induced acidification of CCVs was strikingly reduced in comparison to SVs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 2.

claim: When the coat was removed from CCVs, uncoated vesicles regained ATP-dependent acidification.
source: Remarkably, when the coat was removed from CCVs, uncoated vesicles regained ATP-dependent acidification, demonstrating that CCVs contain the functional vATPase, yet its function is inhibited by the clathrin coat.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: CCVs contain functional vATPase, yet its function is inhibited by the clathrin coat.
source: Remarkably, when the coat was removed from CCVs, uncoated vesicles regained ATP-dependent acidification, demonstrating that CCVs contain the functional vATPase, yet its function is inhibited by the clathrin coat.
evidence: This is inferred from the uncoating experiments and the recovery of acidification.

claim: The formation of the coat surrounds the vATPase and blocks its activity.
source: Considering the known structures of the vATPase and clathrin coat, we propose a model in which the formation of the coat surrounds the vATPase and blocks its activity.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on structural analysis and experimental data.

claim: Clathrin-mediated endocytosis occurs at the synapse.
source: Clathrin-mediated endocytosis is a classic example of vesicle formation mediated by a coat assembly, and it occurs at the synapse (Saheki and De Camilli, 2012; Milosevic, 2018a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Acidification of endocytic compartments is primarily mediated by vATPases.
source: Acidification of endocytic compartments is primarily mediated by vATPases.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cellular acidification mechanisms.

claim: vATPases are large complexes composed of 14 different subunits that are organized into an ATP-hydrolytic domain (V1) and a proton-translocation domain (Vo).
source: These proton pumps are large complexes composed of 14 different subunits that are organized into an ATP-hydrolytic domain (V1) and a proton-translocation domain (Vo) (Imamura et al., 2003; Marshansky et al., 2014; Cotter et al., 2015; Mazhab-Jafari et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: Some studies have suggested that endocytic coated vesicles do not have acidic internal pH.
source: While some have suggested that endocytic coated vesicles do not have acidic internal pH (Anderson et al., 1984; Anderson and Orci, 1988), other studies have shown that membrane-permeable, pH-sensitive, weak bases accumulate in the lumen of CCVs, indicating that acidification occurs in the presence of the coat (Forgac et al., 1983; Van Dyke et al., 1984; Van Dyke et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Other studies have shown that membrane-permeable, pH-sensitive, weak bases accumulate in the lumen of CCVs, indicating that acidification occurs in the presence of the coat.
source: While some have suggested that endocytic coated vesicles do not have acidic internal pH (Anderson et al., 1984; Anderson and Orci, 1988), other studies have shown that membrane-permeable, pH-sensitive, weak bases accumulate in the lumen of CCVs, indicating that acidification occurs in the presence of the coat (Forgac et al., 1983; Van Dyke et al., 1984; Van Dyke et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CCVs were prepared from mouse brain by adapting a published protocol.
source: We have prepared CCVs from mouse brain by adapting a published protocol (Maycox et al., 1992) (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used, citing a previous protocol.

claim: Negative-stained electron microscopy images showed that the CCVs were abundant while almost no uncoated structures were present.
source: Negative-stained electron microscopy (EM) images showed that the CCVs were abundant while almost no uncoated structures were present (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Immunoblotting for organellar marker proteins revealed high enrichment of synaptic vesicle proteins as well as clathrin and clathrin adaptors.
source: Immunoblotting for organellar marker proteins revealed high enrichment of synaptic vesicle proteins as well as clathrin and clathrin adaptors, whereas no significant presence of plasma membrane, endosome and proteasomal proteins was detected (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: No significant presence of plasma membrane, endosome and proteasomal proteins was detected in CCV samples.
source: Immunoblotting for organellar marker proteins revealed high enrichment of synaptic vesicle proteins as well as clathrin and clathrin adaptors, whereas no significant presence of plasma membrane, endosome and proteasomal proteins was detected (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The large majority of CCVs seems to be derived from the synapses.
source: Detailed analysis of CCV samples by mass spectrometry revealed that the large majority of CCVs seems to be derived from the synapses, yet some CCV come from neuronal cell body/intracellular membranes (according to the AP2/AP1 ratio; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: Some CCVs come from neuronal cell body/intracellular membranes according to the AP2/AP1 ratio.
source: Detailed analysis of CCV samples by mass spectrometry revealed that the large majority of CCVs seems to be derived from the synapses, yet some CCV come from neuronal cell body/intracellular membranes (according to the AP2/AP1 ratio; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: Cryo-EM classification of 43,711 individual particles revealed that the majority of vesicles had an intact clathrin coat.
source: Furthermore, cryo-EM classification of 43,711 individual particles revealed that the majority of vesicles had an intact clathrin coat (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The reconstructed CCV structure was comparable in size and symmetry to reconstructed 'barrel-like' empty clathrin cages.
source: The reconstruction from major classes of the imaged particles resulted in a highly symmetric structure (Figure 1D; Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–E)(Video 1), which was comparable in size and symmetry to reconstructed 'barrel-like' empty clathrin cages (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F) (Fotin et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM reconstruction data and comparison to published structures.

claim: The median size of CCVs is in line with previous measurements of CCVs from pig and bovine brains.
source: The median size of CCVs (detailed in Figure 1D for the reconstructed CCV structure and in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C for the population of CCVs) is in line with previous measurements of CCVs from pig and bovine brains (Pearse, 1975; Nossal et al., 1983).
evidence: This is supported by size measurements and citations to previous studies.

claim: Only a minor fluorescence change was detected in CCVs when compared to the respective signals from the SVs upon addition of ATP.
source: Upon addition of ATP, only a minor fluorescence change was detected in CCVs when compared to the respective signals from the SVs (Figure 2C–D), indicating that the ATP-induced change in pH and membrane potential was much smaller in CCVs (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: The ATP-induced change in pH and membrane potential was much smaller in CCVs.
source: Upon addition of ATP, only a minor fluorescence change was detected in CCVs when compared to the respective signals from the SVs (Figure 2C–D), indicating that the ATP-induced change in pH and membrane potential was much smaller in CCVs (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: This is inferred from the fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 2E-F.

claim: The distribution of fluorescence response of single CCVs and SVs clearly showed that the majority of the CCVs did not display any ATP-induced acidification.
source: The distribution of fluorescence response of single CCVs and SVs clearly showed that the majority of the CCVs did not display any ATP-induced acidification (Figure 2G–H).
evidence: This is supported by the distribution data shown in Figure 2G-H.

claim: A subpopulation composed of ~6% of the total CCVs acidified to the same mean extent as SVs.
source: The histogram of luminal pH of CCVs after ATP addition was fit to two Gaussian models revealing that a subpopulation composed of ~6% of the total CCVs acidified to the same mean extent as SVs (Figure 2I–K).
evidence: This is supported by histogram analysis shown in Figure 2I-K.

claim: Acidification of the small subpopulation (~6%) is likely due to the presence of small SV contamination and/or damaged clathrin coats.
source: Acidification of this small subpopulation is likely due to the presence of small SV contamination and/or damaged clathrin coats, as revealed by EM data (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is inferred from EM data showing damaged coats.

claim: A significantly smaller ΔµH+ is formed across the vesicular membrane in the presence of a clathrin coat.
source: Altogether, our data provide evidence that a significantly smaller ∆µH+ is formed across the vesicular membrane in the presence of a clathrin coat.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Delayed kinetics of spH quenching was observed during post-stimulus recovery at living synapses without synaptojanin-1, auxilin or endophilin-A that show delayed uncoating and prominently accumulate CCVs.
source: This finding complements previous studies where delayed kinetics of spH quenching was observed during post-stimulus recovery at living synapses without synaptojanin-1, auxilin or endophilin-A that show delayed uncoating and prominently accumulate CCVs (Mani et al., 2007; Yim et al., 2010; Milosevic et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Both Vo and V1 complex subunits were present on CCVs as well as on SVs.
source: Indeed, both Vo and V1 complex subunits were present on CCVs as well as on SVs.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Lower levels of vATPase subunits as well as other SV proteins were detected in the CCV sample due to the abundance of coat proteins.
source: However, due to the abundance of coat proteins in the CCV samples, we detected lower levels of vATPase subunits as well as other SV proteins in the CCV sample (total protein levels were equal in both samples; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The Vo/V1 ratio was close to one in both SV and CCV samples.
source: The Vo/V1 ratio was close to one in both samples, showing that a complete vATPase complex was present on SVs and CCVs (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A complete vATPase complex was present on SVs and CCVs.
source: The Vo/V1 ratio was close to one in both samples, showing that a complete vATPase complex was present on SVs and CCVs (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is inferred from the Vo/V1 ratio data.

claim: CCVs show significantly less ATPase activity compared to the same amount of SVs.
source: Next, in order to test whether these vATPase complexes are active and able to hydrolyze ATP, we measured the ATPase activity in both CCVs and SVs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), and observed that CCVs show significantly less ATPase activity compared to the same amount of SVs (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by ATPase activity measurements shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The ATPase activity in CCVs was not blocked by N-ethylmaleimide (NEM), an inhibitor of vATPase.
source: In addition, the ATPase activity in CCVs was not blocked by N-ethylmaleimide (NEM), an inhibitor of vATPase, showing that the remaining ATPase activity in CCVs was not due to the vATPase (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by NEM inhibition experiments shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The remaining ATPase activity in CCVs was not due to the vATPase.
source: In addition, the ATPase activity in CCVs was not blocked by N-ethylmaleimide (NEM), an inhibitor of vATPase, showing that the remaining ATPase activity in CCVs was not due to the vATPase (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is inferred from the NEM inhibition data.

claim: The lower ATPase activity measured in CCVs was likely due to impaired function of vATPases in CCVs.
source: These data show that the lower ATPase activity measured in CCVs was likely due to impaired function of vATPases in CCVs.
evidence: This is inferred from the ATPase activity and NEM inhibition data.

claim: vATPases are present on CCVs, but are not able to hydrolyze ATP and pump protons, resulting in inhibited ΔµH+ generation.
source: Taken together, vATPases are present on CCVs, but are not able to hydrolyze ATP and pump protons, resulting in inhibited ∆µH+ generation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Almost all vesicles were uncoated after alkaline Tris-buffer treatment.
source: Firstly, we checked for the uncoating efficiency after alkaline Tris-buffer treatment with negative-staining EM, and observed that almost all vesicles were uncoated (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by EM data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Almost no clathrin HC, clathrin LC, AP2 and AP180 proteins were detected on uncoated vesicles.
source: The immunoblot analysis against clathrin heavy chain (HC) and light chain (LC) as well as adaptor proteins AP180 and AP2 on the uncoated vesicles and in the supernatant after uncoating has revealed that almost no clathrin HC,clathrin LC AP2 and AP180 proteins were detected on uncoated vesicles (all proteins were detected in the supernatant, Figure 4B), providing further evidence for a complete loss of clathrin lattice.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: All clathrin and adaptor proteins were detected in the supernatant after uncoating.
source: The immunoblot analysis against clathrin heavy chain (HC) and light chain (LC) as well as adaptor proteins AP180 and AP2 on the uncoated vesicles and in the supernatant after uncoating has revealed that almost no clathrin HC,clathrin LC AP2 and AP180 proteins were detected on uncoated vesicles (all proteins were detected in the supernatant, Figure 4B), providing further evidence for a complete loss of clathrin lattice.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Uncoated vesicles reached the same luminal pH and membrane potential as SVs upon application of ATP.
source: When ∆pH and ∆ψ in uncoated vesicles was determined, we observed, intriguingly, that uncoated vesicles reached the same luminal pH and membrane potential as SVs upon application of ATP (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: This is supported by measurements shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: No difference in the magnitude of ΔµH+ was observed in Tris-treated SVs.
source: As a control, we performed the same alkaline Tris-buffer treatment with SVs, and observed no difference in the magnitude of ∆µH+ in Tris-treated SVs, ruling out any perturbation caused by alkaline Tris-buffer to the vATPase function (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: This is supported by control experiments shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: Both alternative uncoating treatments successfully uncoated all CCVs as verified by EM.
source: Both treatments have successfully uncoated all CCVs as verified by EM (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), and we have detected full acidification of uncoated vesicles (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by EM data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Full acidification of uncoated vesicles was detected after alternative uncoating treatments.
source: Both treatments have successfully uncoated all CCVs as verified by EM (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), and we have detected full acidification of uncoated vesicles (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by acidification measurements shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The vATPase activity is inhibited in the presence of a fully assembled clathrin coat.
source: Taken together, these experiments demonstrate unequivocally that the vATPase activity is inhibited in the presence of a fully assembled clathrin coat.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the uncoating experiments.

claim: The vATPase inhibition is reversible and the vATPase regains its function once the coat is removed.
source: This inhibition is reversible and the vATPase regains its function once the coat is removed.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the uncoating experiments.

claim: Upon complete hexagonal ring formation, the terminals of clathrin HCs are placed in a very close proximity (<5 nm) to the vesicle membrane.
source: Previously published studies, as well as our cryo-EM analysis of the clathrin coat, have revealed that upon complete hexagonal ring formation, the terminals of clathrin HCs are placed in a very close proximity (<5 nm) to the vesicle membrane (Cheng et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM analysis and citations to previous studies.

claim: Terminal domains of clathrin are suggested to form barrels with diameters ~ 10 nm at the inside surface of the cage.
source: These terminal domains are suggested to form barrels with diameters ~ 10 nm at the inside surface of the cage (our data and Fotin et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis and citations to previous studies.

claim: The neck region of the vATPase (~13 nm) where the regulatory V1H-subunit of the catalytic V1 domain is located would need to be constricted to fit within the clathrin coat.
source: To fit in, the neck region of the vATPase (~13 nm) where the regulatory V1H-subunit of the catalytic V1 domain is located would need to be constricted (for more information, see Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and Suppl data).
evidence: This is inferred from structural modeling and size constraints.

claim: The steric hindrance provided by the formation of the clathrin coat around the vesicles blocks the vATPase activity.
source: Thus, we propose a hypothetical model where the steric hindrance provided by the formation of the clathrin coat around the vesicles blocks the vATPase activity (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Videos 2–4).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on structural analysis and experimental data.

claim: The proposed model is consistent with numerous publications and all experimental data.
source: Such a model is consistent with numerous publications (e.g., Ho et al., 1993; Parra et al., 2000; Jefferies and Forgac, 2008; Diab et al., 2009; Oot and Wilkens, 2012; Oot et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2015; Suzuki et al., 2016; Mazhab-Jafari et al., 2016) and all our data, including the significantly reduced vATPase activity that we observed in isolated CCVs compared to SVs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and experimental data.

claim: The presence of a clathrin coat on the vesicle surface blocks the acidification process during its formation.
source: It also allows for multiple layers of clathrin-coat formation regulation and provides a simple, yet elegant way by which the presence of a clathrin coat on the vesicle surface blocks the acidification process during its formation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the proposed model and experimental data.

claim: Clathrin coat-mediated vATPase inhibition prevents CCV acidification.
source: Our finding that clathrin coat-mediated vATPase inhibition prevents CCV acidification also resolves a longstanding debate in the field.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: The findings require clathrin uncoating upstream of acidification and neurotransmitter refilling in the SV cycle.
source: It contributes to better understanding of the discrete steps of the SV cycle, now requiring clathrin uncoating upstream of acidification and neurotransmitter refilling.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings about CCV acidification.

claim: Even partial formation of the clathrin coat around the vATPase may be sufficient to block its activity.
source: Interestingly, our model suggests that even partial formation of the clathrin coat around the vATPase may be sufficient to block its activity - such regulation may conserve ATP at the synapse.
evidence: This is a speculative inference from the proposed model.

claim: Partial clathrin coat formation may conserve ATP at the synapse.
source: Interestingly, our model suggests that even partial formation of the clathrin coat around the vATPase may be sufficient to block its activity - such regulation may conserve ATP at the synapse.
evidence: This is a speculative inference from the proposed model.

claim: CCVs isolated from brain do not acidify, matching findings in liver CCVs.
source: Finally, our finding that CCVs isolated from brain do not acidify matches findings in liver CCVs (Fuchs et al., 1994), and may provide insight into other cellular processes that involve both clathrin and vATPases.
evidence: This is supported by comparison to previous studies in liver CCVs.

claim: The coated vesicle diameter is 75 nm x 73.5 nm.
source: The median values extracted from the reconstruction of clathrin coat and vesicle within the coat are (note that the structure is a barrel): coated vesicle diameter 75 nm x 73.5 nm, coat thickness 15 nm, vesicle diameter 40 × 35 nm.
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM reconstruction measurements shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The coat thickness is 15 nm.
source: The median values extracted from the reconstruction of clathrin coat and vesicle within the coat are (note that the structure is a barrel): coated vesicle diameter 75 nm x 73.5 nm, coat thickness 15 nm, vesicle diameter 40 × 35 nm.
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM reconstruction measurements shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The vesicle diameter within the coat is 40 × 35 nm.
source: The median values extracted from the reconstruction of clathrin coat and vesicle within the coat are (note that the structure is a barrel): coated vesicle diameter 75 nm x 73.5 nm, coat thickness 15 nm, vesicle diameter 40 × 35 nm.
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM reconstruction measurements shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The V1H-subunit can inhibit the ATPase activity of eukaryotic vATPase when V1 is dissociated from Vo.
source: It is known that the V1H-subunit can inhibit the ATPase activity of eukaryotic vATPase when V1 is dissociated from Vo (Parra et al., 2000; Diab et al., 2009; Jefferies and Forgac, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In holo (VoV1) vATPase the V1H-subunit is required for the ATP hydrolysis.
source: However, in holo (VoV1) vATPase the same subunit is required for the ATP hydrolysis (Jefferies and Forgac, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The dual function of V1H-subunit is dependent on its position relative to the other V1 subunits.
source: Interestingly, recent biochemical and structural studies have revealed that the dual function of V1H-subunit is dependent on its position relative to the other V1 subunits (Jefferies and Forgac, 2008; Oot et al., 2016), and might involve interactions with these subunits (Jefferies and Forgac, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The inhibitory effect of the V1H-subunit is thought to be a result of its rotation towards V1D and V1F.
source: Further, the inhibitory effect of the V1H-subunit is thought to be a result of its rotation towards V1D (Oot et al., 2016) and V1F (Jefferies and Forgac, 2008), which compose the central rotor of the complex (Marshansky et al., 2014; Zhao et al., 2015; Mazhab-Jafari et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: V1D and V1F compose the central rotor of the vATPase complex.
source: Further, the inhibitory effect of the V1H-subunit is thought to be a result of its rotation towards V1D (Oot et al., 2016) and V1F (Jefferies and Forgac, 2008), which compose the central rotor of the complex (Marshansky et al., 2014; Zhao et al., 2015; Mazhab-Jafari et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The steric hindrance results in dislocation of the regulatory V1H-subunit towards the stalk.
source: Thus, we propose a model where the steric hindrance provided by the formation of the clathrin coat around the vesicles results in dislocation of the regulatory V1H-subunit towards the stalk (Figure 4G; Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Videos 2–4).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on structural analysis.

claim: The displacement of the regulatory V1H-subunit closer to the other V1 subunits would block the activity of the proton pump.
source: The displacement of the regulatory V1H-subunit respectively closer to the other V1 subunits, most probably V1D and Vod, and in turn would block the activity of the proton pump as suggested by several publications (Diab et al., 2009; Jefferies and Forgac, 2008; Oot and Wilkens, 2012; Zhao et al., 2015; Suzuki et al., 2016; Mazhab-Jafari et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism supported by citations to previous literature.
